rv.q: In The Prisoner, Peter Brook’s new work with long-term collaborator Marie-Helene Estienne, they turn their eyes on the exotic – but the result reveals a lot more about them, than the things they are looking at. It is tempting to position this as a great statement by a revered figure of the theatre.

Half an hour passed between the two of us, during which time I was treated to Zeus’s witless epigrams that I am sure were meant to make me feel inadequate. “War is a state of mind.” “Reality is the limit of your existence.” “Muesli is the cement of my intellect.” Anyway, I thought of Zeus when I saw Peter Brook’s latest work, The Prisoner.
Despite the vivid subject matter, An Execution (By Invitation Only) lacks context; it is devoid of politics, class and wit.

How do you know when you have punished yourself enough? Despite the piece being poignantly acted by Hiran Abeysekera as Mavuso, who manages to chug the story along at a steady pace, the production falls flat when it aims for depth and symbolism.
